Subject: Network connectivity options for Redwood Private deploy (NovaHealth)

Hi Marissa,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — our security and cloud teams asked me to get a clear recommendation from Redwood on the connectivity approach for a Private deployment. Our constraints: HIPAA environment, multi-account org (prod + data ingest), some workloads in us-east-1 and us-west-2, and a steady inference throughput (we expect bursts up to ~3k rps). Key concerns are:

- Data egress patterns and cost between accounts/regions
- Compliance (no public internet egress for PHI)
- Failover and predictable latency SLAs

Can you provide a short write-up comparing VPC peering vs AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) vs site-to-site VPN (managed S2S with BGP) for this profile? We attached our short network questionnaire (novahealth-network-questionnaire.pdf) — happy to schedule a deeper technical call.

Also can you include a recommended default for production vs. a low-cost staging option and any rough cost direction (ballpark is fine)?

Thanks,
Paula
Director, Cloud Ops — NovaHealth

Hi Paula — appreciate the clear constraints. I pushed a concise comparison and recommendation into the attached playbook and spreadsheet (vpc-connectivity-playbook-v1.pdf, connectivity-pros-cons.xlsx). High level:

- TL;DR recommended production default: AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoint) for the Redwood control plane + dedicated ENIs for model endpoints; pair with VPC peering inside a single region/account where very high-volume data transfer happens.
- Staging/PoC default: Site-to-site VPN (managed) to lower up-front complexity; acceptable for latency-tolerant testing but not ideal for sustained high throughput.

Why this mix? PrivateLink gives you strong security boundaries (no public IPs, cross-account access control, and fine-grained endpoint policies), and avoids transitive routing issues. VPC peering is cheaper for same-account or same-region high-throughput communication but lacks the fine-grained access controls of PrivateLink. S2S VPN is useful as a short-term or DR path.

Next steps I suggest:
1) Quick triage workshop with your cloud/networking folks + our infra engineer (Karthik) to validate route tables, TGW assumptions, and expected egress volumes.
2) Pilot the PrivateLink interface in one region for control plane traffic and run a 48h throughput test.
3) If bulk data moves are large, measure peering path costs and consider cross-region peering for those flows.

I've cc'd Karthik to add technical detail and Rishi for cost/pricing guidance. Can you propose 2 times for a 60m workshop next week?

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Paula / team — adding a short technical supplement with implementation tradeoffs and gotchas we often see. High level bullets below; details are in the playbook attachment Marissa shared.

- VPC Peering
  - Pros: Lower per-packet overhead, straightforward routing inside AWS, can be less expensive for very high-volume intra-region transfer because data can stay on AWS backbone.
  - Cons: Not transitive (requires point-to-point peering for each VPC), cross-account peering needs explicit route management, can get messy at scale with many VPCs. Not ideal for exposing a managed service API across many accounts without a centralization pattern (e.g., Transit Gateway).
  - Notes: Cross-region peering exists but adds cost; watch route table explosion and NACL/security group maintenance.

- AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints)
  - Pros: Cross-account-friendly, no public internet exposure (good for PHI), endpoint policies allow least-privilege access, simple DNS and IAM integration; fits well with a service-provider model (Redwood runs behind NLB -> PrivateLink).
  - Cons: You pay per-hour per-endpoint + per-GB data processing charges; requires managing ENIs and ENI IPs in peered VPCs; also regional — cross-region requires separate endpoints.
  - Notes: PrivateLink avoids transitive routing headaches and integrates cleanly with customer KMS and endpoint policies for compliance. For high-throughput ML inference, ensure the underlying NLB and backend instances are sized and you enable enhanced networking.

- Site-to-Site VPN (managed with BGP)
  - Pros: Fast to stand up, works across cloud providers and on-prem, supports BGP for route failover, can be used as a DR/fallback path.
  - Cons: Higher latency and jitter compared to native AWS backbone; throughput caps on individual tunnels unless you leverage multiple tunnels or AWS Accelerated VPN; operational complexity for stable high-throughput inference.
  - Notes: MTU and fragmentation issues are common for inference payloads — ensure path MTU discovery or tune MSS on endpoints.

Recommended pattern for NovaHealth given HIPAA and multi-account:
1) Primary: PrivateLink for Redwood control plane + model endpoints (per-region). This gives you the clean security posture and access control.
2) For intra-account heavy data movement (e.g., large dataset replication), use VPC peering or Transit Gateway inside the account/region to avoid the per-GB PrivateLink processing fees.
3) Use a managed S2S VPN (or Direct Connect if procurement allows) only for staging or as a DR/fallback path — not as the primary production path for latency-sensitive inference.

Operational checklist items to validate in the workshop:
- Confirm region pairs for production endpoints and whether cross-region active/active is required.
- Estimate persistent vs burst throughput so we can size NLBs and endpoint bandwidth.
- Agree on logging/audit plan (flow logs, endpoint logs) for compliance evidence.
- Decide whether a Transit Gateway will be used (helps at scale but adds cost and routing considerations).

I'll draft a short runbook for the pilot after the workshop.
